facts.statement: The initial specimen of Archaeopteryx was the first dinosaur discovered with feathers.

facts.statement: A single feather, the initial discovery of Archaeopteryx, was unearthed in 1860 or 1861 and described in 1861 by Hermann von Meyer.
facts.quote: The initial discovery, a single feather, was unearthed in 1860 or 1861 and described in 1861 by Hermann von Meyer.

facts.statement: In 2019, laser imaging revealed that the initial feather specimen was inconsistent with other known Archaeopteryx feathers, leading to a conclusion that it originated from another dinosaur.
facts.quote: In 2019 it was reported that laser imaging had revealed the structure of the quill (which had not been visible since some time after the feather was described), and that the feather was inconsistent with the morphology of all other Archaeopteryx feathers known, leading to the conclusion that it originated from another dinosaur.

facts.statement: In 2020, researchers challenged the conclusion that the initial feather was from another dinosaur, identifying it morphologically as an upper major primary covert feather.
facts.quote: This conclusion was challenged in 2020 as being unlikely; the feather was identified on the basis of morphology as most likely having been an upper major primary covert feather.

facts.statement: The first skeleton, known as the London Specimen, was unearthed in 1861 near Langenaltheim, Germany, and may have been given to physician Karl Häberlein in exchange for medical services.
facts.quote: The first skeleton, known as the London Specimen (BMNH 37001), was unearthed in 1861 near Langenaltheim, Germany, and perhaps given to local physician Karl Häberlein in return for medical services.

facts.statement: The London Specimen was sold for £700 (roughly £83,000 in 2020) to the Natural History Museum in London, where it remains.
facts.quote: He then sold it for £700 (roughly £83,000 in 2020) to the Natural History Museum in London, where it remains.

facts.statement: The London Specimen, missing most of its head and neck, was described in 1863 by Richard Owen as Archaeopteryx macrura.
facts.quote: Missing most of its head and neck, it was described in 1863 by Richard Owen as Archaeopteryx macrura, allowing for the possibility it did not belong to the same species as the feather.

facts.statement: The Berlin Specimen was discovered in 1874 or 1875 on the Blumenberg near Eichstätt, Germany, by farmer Jakob Niemeyer.
facts.quote: The Berlin Specimen (HMN 1880/81) was discovered in 1874 or 1875 on the Blumenberg near Eichstätt, Germany, by farmer Jakob Niemeyer.

facts.statement: Jakob Niemeyer sold the Berlin Specimen in 1876 to buy a cow, and it was subsequently sold to Ernst Otto Häberlein.
facts.quote: He sold this precious fossil for the money to buy a cow in 1876, to innkeeper Johann Dörr, who again sold it to Ernst Otto Häberlein, the son of K. Häberlein.

facts.statement: The Berlin Specimen was bought for 20,000 Goldmark by the Berlin Natural History Museum between 1877 and 1881.
facts.quote: Placed on sale between 1877 and 1881, with potential buyers including O. C. Marsh of Yale University's Peabody Museum, it eventually was bought for 20,000 Goldmark by the Berlin's Natural History Museum, where it now is displayed.

facts.statement: The purchase of the Berlin Specimen was financed by Ernst Werner von Siemens.
facts.quote: The transaction was financed by Ernst Werner von Siemens, founder of the company that bears his name.

facts.statement: The Berlin Specimen was described in 1884 by Wilhelm Dames and is the most complete specimen with a complete head.
facts.quote: Described in 1884 by Wilhelm Dames, it is the most complete specimen, and the first with a complete head.

facts.statement: In 1897, Wilhelm Dames named the Berlin Specimen as the new species A. siemensii, though some 21st-century studies consider it a distinct species including the Berlin, Munich, and Thermopolis specimens.
facts.quote: In 1897 it was named by Dames as a new species, A. siemensii; though often considered a synonym of A. lithographica, several 21st century studies have concluded that it is a distinct species which includes the Berlin, Munich, and Thermopolis specimens.

facts.statement: The Maxberg Specimen was discovered in 1956 near Langenaltheim and described by Florian Heller in 1959.
facts.quote: The Maxberg Specimen (S5) was discovered in 1956 near Langenaltheim; it was brought to the attention of the German paleontologist Florian Heller in 1958 and described by him in 1959.

facts.statement: The Haarlem Specimen was discovered in 1855 near Riedenburg, Germany, and described as Pterodactylus crassipes in 1857 by Meyer.
facts.quote: The "Haarlem Specimen" (TM 6428/29, also known as the Teylers Specimen) was discovered in 1855 near Riedenburg, Germany, and described as a Pterodactylus crassipes in 1857 by Meyer.

facts.statement: The Haarlem Specimen was reclassified in 1970 by John Ostrom and is located at the Teylers Museum in Haarlem, the Netherlands.
facts.quote: It was reclassified in 1970 by John Ostrom and is currently located at the Teylers Museum in Haarlem, the Netherlands.

facts.statement: In 2017, the Haarlem Specimen was named the separate genus Ostromia, a decision criticized for over-interpreting traits of the poorly preserved fossil.
facts.quote: In 2017 it was named as a separate genus Ostromia, considered more closely related to Anchiornis from China; this decision was subsequently criticized as being based on over-interpretating some spurious traits of the old and badly-preserved fossil.

facts.statement: The Eichstätt Specimen was discovered in 1951 near Workerszell, Germany, and described by Peter Wellnhofer in 1974.
facts.quote: The Eichstätt Specimen (JM 2257) was discovered in 1951 near Workerszell, Germany, and described by Peter Wellnhofer in 1974.

facts.statement: The Eichstätt Specimen is the smallest known specimen and possesses the second-best head preservation.
facts.quote: Currently located at the Jura Museum in Eichstätt, Germany, it is the smallest known specimen and has the second-best head.

facts.statement: In 2007, Phil Senter suggested that Jurapteryx, A. siemensii, and A. bavarica are junior synonyms of A. lithographica, arguing that their diagnostic features can be explained by ontogeny.
facts.quote: In 2007, Phil Senter classified Jurapteryx, A. siemensii and A. bavarica as junior synonyms of A. lithographica, suggesting that proposed diagnostic features of these taxa based on proportional and dental differences can be explained by ontogeny.

facts.statement: The Unnumbered Specimen was discovered in the 1970s near Eichstätt, Germany, and described in 1988 by Wellnhofer.
facts.quote: The ('Unnumbered Specimen') was discovered in the 1970s near Eichstätt, Germany, and described in 1988 by Wellnhofer.

facts.statement: The Munich Specimen was discovered on August 3, 1992, near Langenaltheim and described in 1993 by Wellnhofer.
facts.quote: The Munich Specimen (BSP 1999 I 50, formerly known as the Solenhofer-Aktien-Verein Specimen) was discovered on 3 August 1992 near Langenaltheim and described in 1993 by Wellnhofer.

facts.statement: A fragmentary fossil known as the Bürgermeister-Müller Specimen was found in 2000.
facts.quote: Another fragmentary fossil was found in 2000.

facts.statement: The Thermopolis Specimen was discovered in Bavaria and described in 2005 by Mayr, Pohl, and Peters.
facts.quote: The Thermopolis Specimen (WDC CSG 100) was discovered in Bavaria and described in 2005 by Mayr, Pohl, and Peters.

facts.statement: The eleventh specimen, known as the Altmühl Specimen, was announced in 2011 and described in 2014.
facts.quote: The discovery of an eleventh specimen was announced in 2011; it was described in 2014.

facts.statement: The Schamhaupten Specimen was discovered by an amateur collector in 2010 at the Schamhaupten quarry and announced in February 2014.
facts.quote: The Schamhaupten Specimen had been discovered by an amateur collector in 2010 at the Schamhaupten quarry, but the finding was only announced in February 2014.

facts.statement: The Karlsruhe Specimen, a thirteenth specimen, was published in January 2025 from the Mörnsheim Formation.
facts.quote: A thirteenth specimen, SMNK-PAL 10,000 or Karlsruhe Specimen, was published in January 2025, this one from the Mörnsheim Formation.

facts.statement: The Schamhaupten Specimen is the only known specimen lacking preserved feathers.
facts.quote: It is the only specimen lacking preserved feathers.

facts.statement: The Mühlheim Specimen was initially considered a thirteenth Archaeopteryx but was reassigned to the distinct genus Alcmonavis upon its 2019 description.
facts.quote: When the specimen was scientifically described in 2019, it was thus reassigned to a distinct genus Alcmonavis.

facts.statement: The Unnumbered Specimen was originally classified as Compsognathus by the amateur collector Friedrich Müller.
facts.quote: It originally was classified as Compsognathus by an amateur collector, the same mayor Friedrich Müller after which the museum is named.

facts.statement: The Schamhaupten Specimen is from the Painten Formation and is somewhat older than other Archaeopteryx specimens.
facts.quote: It is from the Painten Formation and somewhat older than the other specimens.

facts.statement: In 1985, an amateur group led by Fred Hoyle and Lee Spetner claimed that the feathers on the Berlin and London Archaeopteryx specimens were forged.
facts.quote: Beginning in 1985, an amateur group including astronomer Fred Hoyle and physicist Lee Spetner, published a series of papers claiming that the feathers on the Berlin and London specimens of Archaeopteryx were forged.

facts.statement: Alan J. Charig and colleagues cited hairline cracks running through both rock and fossil impressions, along with pre-discovery mineral growth, as evidence that the feathers were original.
facts.quote: Charig et al. pointed to the presence of hairline cracks in the slabs running through both rock and fossil impressions, and mineral growth over the slabs that had occurred before discovery and preparation, as evidence that the feathers were original.

facts.statement: Archaeopteryx was roughly the size of a raven, featuring broad wings with rounded ends and a long tail relative to its body length.
facts.quote: Archaeopteryx was roughly the size of a raven, with broad wings that were rounded at the ends and a long tail compared to its body length.

facts.statement: Unlike modern birds, Archaeopteryx possessed small teeth and a long bony tail, features shared with other dinosaurs of its time.
facts.quote: Unlike modern birds, Archaeopteryx had small teeth, as well as a long bony tail, features which Archaeopteryx shared with other dinosaurs of the time.

facts.statement: Archaeopteryx specimens are notable for well-developed, markedly asymmetrical flight feathers with vanes stabilized by a barb-barbule-barbicel arrangement similar to modern birds.
facts.quote: Specimens of Archaeopteryx were most notable for their well-developed flight feathers. They were markedly asymmetrical and showed the structure of flight feathers in modern birds, with vanes given stability by a barb-barbule-barbicel arrangement.

facts.statement: A patch of symmetrical and firm pennaceous feathers ran along the back of Archaeopteryx, similar to modern bird contour feathers but less stiff than flight feathers.
facts.quote: A patch of pennaceous feathers is found running along its back, which was quite similar to the contour feathers of the body plumage of modern birds in being symmetrical and firm, although not as stiff as the flight-related feathers.

facts.statement: Most Archaeopteryx specimens likely drifted on their backs in the sea before becoming embedded in anoxic sediment, resulting in a characteristic "death pose" with the head, neck, and tail bent downward due to muscle relaxation and early decomposition.
facts.quote: It appears that most Archaeopteryx specimens became embedded in anoxic sediment after drifting some time on their backs in the sea—the head, neck and the tail are generally bent downward, which suggests that the specimens had just started to rot when they were embedded, with tendons and muscle relaxing so that the characteristic shape (death pose) of the fossil specimens was achieved.

facts.statement: The forgery hypothesis proposed by Hoyle and Spetner has not been taken seriously by paleontologists because their evidence was based on geological misunderstandings and ignored other feather-bearing specimens.
facts.quote: Their suggestions have not been taken seriously by palaeontologists, as their evidence was largely based on misunderstandings of geology, and they never discussed the other feather-bearing specimens, which have increased in number since then.

facts.statement: A 2011 study used scanning electron microscopy to analyze a single isolated feather from an Archaeopteryx specimen.
facts.quote: In 2011, graduate student Ryan Carney and colleagues performed the first colour study on an Archaeopteryx specimen.

facts.statement: Comparisons with 87 modern bird species led researchers to calculate a 95% likelihood that the analyzed feather was originally black.
facts.quote: The resultant measurements were then compared to those of 87 modern bird species, and the original colour was calculated with a 95% likelihood to be black.

facts.statement: Gavin de Beer concluded in 1954 that the London specimen served as the holotype for the genus.
facts.quote: In 1954 Gavin de Beer concluded that the London specimen was the holotype.

facts.statement: In 2007, scientists petitioned the ICZN to designate the London specimen as the neotype to resolve nomenclatorial confusion.
facts.quote: In 2007, two sets of scientists therefore petitioned the ICZN requesting that the London specimen explicitly be made the type by designating it as the new holotype specimen, or neotype.

facts.statement: The ICZN upheld the suggestion after four years of debate and designated the London specimen as the neotype on October 3, 2011.
facts.quote: This suggestion was upheld by the ICZN after four years of debate, and the London specimen was designated the neotype on 3 October 2011.

facts.statement: In 1960, Swinton proposed placing Archaeopteryx lithographica on the official genera list, rendering alternative names like Griphosaurus and Griphornis invalid.
facts.quote: In 1960, Swinton accordingly proposed that the name Archaeopteryx lithographica be placed on the official genera list making the alternative names Griphosaurus and Griphornis invalid.

facts.statement: A 2007 review concluded that two distinct species, A. lithographica and A. siemensii, could be supported based on well-preserved specimens including the Thermopolis find.
facts.quote: In 2007, a review of all well-preserved specimens including the then-newly discovered Thermopolis specimen concluded that two distinct species of Archaeopteryx could be supported: A. lithographica (consisting of at least the London and Solnhofen specimens), and A. siemensii (consisting of at least the Berlin, Munich, and Thermopolis specimens).

facts.statement: The proposed species Wellnhoferia grandis, based on the Solnhofen specimen, appears indistinguishable from A. lithographica except for its larger size.
facts.quote: A supposed additional species, Wellnhoferia grandis (based on the Solnhofen specimen), seems to be indistinguishable from A. lithographica except in its larger size.

facts.statement: The valid name for the species is Archaeopteryx lithographica, described by Meyer in 1861 and designated a conserved name.
facts.quote: Archaeopteryx lithographica Meyer, 1861 [conserved name]

facts.statement: The name Griphosaurus problematicus, proposed by Wagner in 1862, was rejected in 1961 by the ICZN.
facts.quote: Griphosaurus problematicus Wagner, 1862 [rejected name 1961 per ICZN Opinion 607]

facts.statement: The species Archaeopteryx siemensii was described by Dames in 1897.
facts.quote: Archaeopteryx siemensii Dames, 1897

facts.statement: The species Archaeopteryx bavarica was described by Wellnhofer in 1993.
facts.quote: Archaeopteryx bavarica Wellnhofer, 1993

facts.statement: It is debated whether biomarkers found in the feather can accurately indicate eumelanin coloration across the entire Archaeopteryx specimen.
facts.quote: An author on the previous Archaeopteryx colour study argued against the interpretation of such biomarkers as an indicator of eumelanin in the full Archaeopteryx specimen.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the first described specimen, a single feather, corresponds well with the flight feathers of the rest of the Archaeopteryx fossils.
facts.quote: It has been noted that the feather, the first specimen of Archaeopteryx described, does not correspond well with the flight-related feathers of Archaeopteryx.

facts.statement: Researchers debate whether the first described feather belongs to Archaeopteryx or to another, smaller species of feathered theropod.
facts.quote: It certainly is a flight feather of a contemporary species, but its size and proportions indicate that it may belong to another, smaller species of feathered theropod, of which only this feather is known so far.

facts.statement: It is debated whether all known specimens belong to the single species A. lithographica or represent multiple species.
facts.quote: It has been argued that all the specimens belong to the same species, A. lithographica.

facts.statement: It is debated whether differences among specimens are due to age variations or represent actual species diversity.
facts.quote: Differences do exist among the specimens, and while some researchers regard these as due to the different ages of the specimens, some may be related to actual species diversity.

facts.statement: Modern paleontology often classifies Archaeopteryx as the most primitive bird.
facts.quote: Modern palaeontology has often classified Archaeopteryx as the most primitive bird.

facts.statement: Lowe (1935) and Thulborn (1984) questioned whether Archaeopteryx was truly the first bird.
facts.quote: Lowe (1935) and Thulborn (1984) questioned whether Archaeopteryx truly was the first bird.

facts.statement: Some researchers suggested that Archaeopteryx was a dinosaur no more closely related to birds than other dinosaur groups.
facts.quote: They suggested that Archaeopteryx was a dinosaur that was no more closely related to birds than were other dinosaur groups.

facts.statement: Kurzanov (1987) suggested that Avimimus was a more likely ancestor of all birds than Archaeopteryx.
facts.quote: Kurzanov (1987) suggested that Avimimus was more likely to be the ancestor of all birds than Archaeopteryx.

facts.statement: A subsequent thorough analysis found Archaeopteryx at the base of Avialae and Xiaotingia as a basal dromaeosaurid or troodontid, contradicting the deinonychosaur hypothesis.
facts.quote: A more thorough analysis was published soon after to test this hypothesis, and failed to arrive at the same result; it found Archaeopteryx in its traditional position at the base of Avialae, while Xiaotingia was recovered as a basal dromaeosaurid or troodontid.

facts.statement: Researchers noted that it may not be possible to confidently determine if Archaeopteryx is a member of Avialae without new and better specimens.
facts.quote: The authors of the follow-up study noted that uncertainties still exist, and that it may not be possible to state confidently whether or not Archaeopteryx is a member of Avialae or not, barring new and better specimens of relevant species.

facts.statement: Hu et al. (2018), Wang et al. (2018), and Hartman et al. (2019) found Archaeopteryx to be a deinonychosaur instead of an avialan.
facts.quote: Hu et al. (2018), Wang et al. (2018) and Hartman et al. (2019) found Archaeopteryx to have been a deinonychosaur instead of an avialan.

facts.statement: Hartman et al. considered it highly probable that Archaeopteryx evolved flight independently from bird ancestors, Microraptor, and Yi.
facts.quote: Because Hartman et al. found Archaeopteryx isolated in a group of flightless deinonychosaurs (otherwise considered "anchiornithids"), they considered it highly probable that this animal evolved flight independently from bird ancestors (and from Microraptor and Yi).

facts.statement: Archaeopteryx possessed asymmetrical flight feathers and broad tail feathers similar to modern birds.
facts.quote: As in the wings of modern birds, the flight feathers of Archaeopteryx were somewhat asymmetrical and the tail feathers were rather broad.

facts.statement: A 2006 study by Philip Senter suggested Archaeopteryx could not flap like modern birds but might have used a downstroke-only gliding technique.
facts.quote: According to a study by Philip Senter in 2006, Archaeopteryx was indeed unable to use flapping flight as modern birds do, but it may well have used a downstroke-only flap-assisted gliding technique.

facts.statement: A 2010 study by Nudds and Dyke analyzed feather rachises and suggested Archaeopteryx was unable to use flapping flight.
facts.quote: In 2010, Robert L. Nudds and Gareth J. Dyke in the journal Science published a paper in which they analysed the rachises of the primary feathers of Confuciusornis and Archaeopteryx. The analysis suggested that the rachises on these two genera were thinner and weaker than those of modern birds relative to body mass.

facts.statement: Gregory Paul disputed the 2010 findings, arguing that corrected mass estimates would allow Archaeopteryx to achieve powered flight.
facts.quote: Gregory Paul also disagreed with the study, arguing in a 2010 response that Nudds and Dyke had overestimated the masses of these early birds, and that more accurate mass estimates allowed powered flight even with relatively narrow rachises.

facts.statement: Archaeopteryx had asymmetrical flight feathers on its legs, similar to dromaeosaurids, which likely aided its aerial mobility.
facts.quote: The presence of "hind wings", asymmetrical flight feathers stemming from the legs similar to those seen in dromaeosaurids such as Microraptor, also would have added to the aerial mobility of Archaeopteryx.

facts.statement: A 2006 study found that Archaeopteryx's leg feathers formed up to 12% of its total airfoil.
facts.quote: The first detailed study of the hind wings by Longrich in 2006, suggested that the structures formed up to 12% of the total airfoil.

facts.statement: Researchers disagree on feather measurements, with Nudds and Dyke reporting a 0.75 mm diameter while Paul measured inner rachises at 1.25–1.4 mm.
facts.quote: Nudds and Dyke reported a diameter of 0.75 mm for the longest primary feather, which Paul could not confirm using photographs. Paul measured some of the inner primary feathers, finding rachises 1.25–1.4 mm across.

facts.statement: A 2004 CT scan of the London specimen showed Archaeopteryx had a significantly larger brain than most dinosaurs, indicating it had the brain size necessary for flight.
facts.quote: In 2004, scientists analysing a detailed CT scan of the braincase of the London Archaeopteryx concluded that its brain was significantly larger than that of most dinosaurs, indicating that it possessed the brain size necessary for flying.

facts.statement: Reconstruction of the London specimen's brain showed vision-related regions occupied nearly one-third of the brain volume.
facts.quote: The reconstruction showed that the regions associated with vision took up nearly one-third of the brain.

facts.statement: Recent studies show Archaeopteryx lacked the large trailing barb angle found in modern birds, indicating potentially weak flight abilities.
facts.quote: Recent studies of flight feather barb geometry reveal that modern birds possess a larger barb angle in the trailing vane of the feather, whereas Archaeopteryx lacks this large barb angle, indicating potentially weak flight abilities.

facts.statement: Scientists debate whether Archaeopteryx was a tree-dwelling glider ('trees down' hypothesis) or a ground-runner ('ground up' hypothesis).
facts.quote: Some scientists see it as a semi-arboreal climbing animal, following the idea that birds evolved from tree-dwelling gliders (the "trees down" hypothesis for the evolution of flight proposed by O. C. Marsh). Other scientists see Archaeopteryx as running quickly along the ground, supporting the idea that birds evolved flight by running (the "ground up" hypothesis proposed by Samuel Wendell Williston).

facts.statement: A 2002 scenario suggests Archaeopteryx used glides punctuated with shallow downstrokes to escape predators and cover distances.
facts.quote: A scenario outlined by Elżanowski in 2002 suggested that Archaeopteryx used its wings mainly to escape predators by glides punctuated with shallow downstrokes to reach successively higher perches, and alternatively, to cover longer distances (mainly) by gliding down from cliffs or treetops.

facts.statement: A 2018 study reported Archaeopteryx had a flight stroke cycle closer to the grabbing motion of maniraptorans than modern birds.
facts.quote: In March 2018, scientists reported that Archaeopteryx was likely capable of a flight stroke cycle morphologically closer to the grabbing motion of maniraptorans and distinct from that of modern birds.

facts.statement: A 2026 CT study of the Chicago specimen found avian-like soft tissue structures in the feeding apparatus, including oral papillae and a mobile tongue.
facts.quote: 2026 CT-based study of the Chicago Archaeopteryx specimen reported avian-like soft-tissue correlates in the feeding apparatus, including structures interpreted as oral papillae and elements of a mobile tongue, suggesting similarities with feeding adaptations seen in modern birds.

facts.statement: Archaeopteryx most likely hunted small prey by seizing it with its jaws or claws.
facts.quote: It most likely hunted small prey, seizing it with its jaws or claws

facts.statement: The genus includes the species A. albersdoerferi (Kundrat et al. 2018), A. lithographica (Meyer, 1861), and A. siemensii (Dames, 1897).
facts.quote: subdivision: * A. albersdoerferi Kundrat et al. 2018 A. lithographica Meyer, 1861 (tipo) A. siemensii Dames, 1897
